Project 01 / WEB & MOBILE · CAPSTONE PROJECT
GCS
Ground Control Station
GCS smart mosquito control drone hero image
A web-based ground control station and mobile companion app for a smart mosquito control drone, bringing flight monitoring and mission information into connected interfaces.
Design focus
Make flight information, live camera feeds, and detection data understandable within one clear operator workflow.
Full-Stack Web & Mobile Developer
Computer Engineering Capstone Project
Completed · Currently offline
React · TypeScript · Node.js · Supabase · UDP · Figma · Visual Studio Code · GitHub
The challenge

The project required an interface that could make a complex hardware-and-software system understandable to its operator. Flight information, a live camera feed, and mosquito breeding-site detection needed to fit into a clear workflow.
The challenge was deciding which information deserved immediate attention, how to organize controls around the operator’s tasks, and how the mobile app could support the experience.
Mapping the experience

I mapped the system’s workflows to understand how users would move between flight monitoring, detection information, and flight history. These flows helped define the screen structure, navigation, and placement of key information.
Separating active monitoring from reviewing past flights also helped establish the responsibilities of the web dashboard and mobile companion app.
GCS web dashboard showing the main flight monitoring workspace
GCS mobile dashboard showing a focused companion view
Design decisions
GCS web stream view with camera feed and detection information
Web and mobile, with different jobs
The web application serves as the main control and monitoring workspace, while the mobile app focuses on checking flight details and history.

The larger web interface provides room for the live feed, flight information, and controls to appear together. Mobile prioritizes a focused view of flight records and details that users can access without opening the full dashboard.
This division gives each platform a clear purpose while maintaining consistent terminology and visual patterns.

What I learned

This project taught me to approach interface design alongside system behavior. In a connected hardware-and-software project, the usefulness of a screen depends on how clearly it communicates the data and functionality behind it.
Working across web and mobile also helped me think more carefully about information priority and the purpose of each platform.

The capstone is complete, but the applications are currently offline. Future improvements would include clearer connection and error states, stronger visual hierarchy, and usability testing to evaluate how easily users understand the monitoring workflow.
Project 02 / FASHION · IN DEVELOPMENT
Off the Rack
Fashion Catalog & Brand Website

A responsive fashion catalog for my independent brand, featuring curated denim, hand-painted pieces, and upcycled streetwear. Customers can discover one-of-one products, explore sold pieces, and submit purchase inquiries, with a separate admin experience for catalog and inquiry management.
Design focus
Connect a distinctive fashion identity with clear product discovery, availability, and purchase inquiries.
Founder, UI/UX Designer and Web Developer
Personal Brand Website and Digital Catalog
In Development
Figma · Next.js · Supabase · Supabase Auth · GitHub · Vercel
The challenge

Off the Rack sells one-of-one pieces rather than products that can be continuously restocked. A typical e-commerce flow could create confusion when an item becomes unavailable or when payment and delivery details still need to be confirmed manually.

The challenge was to create a polished, easy-to-browse shopping experience that supports a small handmade fashion business: communicate availability, preserve sold pieces as a creative archive, and give the administrator a practical way to manage products and inquiries.
Platform: Responsive WebScope: Customer Storefront and Admin Dashboard
Mapping the experience
I divided the experience into two connected sides: the customer storefront and the admin dashboard.
Customer experience
Discover → Browse → View product → Submit inquiry → Receive confirmation

Visitors can explore featured pieces, browse and filter the catalog, open product pages, and inquire about an available item. Sold products move into the Archive, where they continue to represent the brand’s previous work and visual identity.
Admin experience
Sign in → Review dashboard → Manage products → Update availability → Handle inquiries

The admin workflow covers creating and editing products, organizing categories, changing availability, archiving sold items, and reviewing inquiries. Separating these tools from the storefront keeps management focused behind authenticated access.

Design decisions
Treating the website as a digital lookbook
Large product imagery, editorial layouts, and restrained typography let the customized denim carry the visual identity. The interface is designed to feel like an independent fashion label.
Using inquiries instead of checkout
Every product is unique, and payment or delivery may require direct confirmation. An inquiry-based purchasing flow gives interested customers a clear next step that fits how the business operates.
Keeping sold pieces visible
Sold items belong in an Archive instead of being removed. This creates a growing portfolio of the brand’s work while clearly separating previous pieces from available products.
Separating customer and admin tasks
The storefront prioritizes discovery and product presentation; the dashboard prioritizes inventory and inquiry management. Each side has a distinct purpose.
Building reusable patterns
Product cards, category filters, status labels, form elements, and dashboard controls follow reusable visual patterns to keep the interface consistent as the catalog grows.

Shop, product details, and Archive

The shop is designed around search, filters, sorting, and availability indicators. Product pages provide larger imagery, sizing or condition details, and a direct path to inquire. The Archive preserves sold pieces without presenting them as available. The shop and product layouts are shown in the initial wireframes above.
Inquiry flow

The inquiry form collects contact details and product interest so availability, payment, and delivery can be confirmed manually. The contact page also provides paths for general questions and custom requests.

Admin dashboard and catalog management

The dashboard provides an overview of products, inventory status, and inquiries. Category management organizes the catalog. Product and inquiry management workflows cover creating, editing, archiving, and removing products, as well as reviewing requests and tracking their status.
Current interface — admin dashboard with an empty catalog
Current interface — category management
What I learned
Designing for a real small business requires understanding how it actually operates instead of automatically copying standard e-commerce patterns.

Inquiries, availability statuses, and a sold-item archive came directly from the one-of-one nature of the products. They showed me how information architecture and status logic can prevent confusion for both customers and administrators.

Designing the admin workflows alongside the customer journey also helped me consider the complete system: how content, inventory, and inquiries move through the platform behind the visible storefront.
Limitations and next steps
The platform does not currently include online checkout or payment processing. Orders, payment, and delivery arrangements are confirmed manually after an inquiry is submitted.

Product image uploading is the next step for the live site. Future improvements may include image storage, email notifications, analytics, inventory alerts, inquiry status updates, and usability testing with potential customers.
Project 03 / GAME UI · SELF-INITIATED CONCEPT
Riftbound
Pixel RPG Interface Design
Riftbound pixel RPG interface concept hero artwork
A personal game UI/UX concept exploring how pixel-art visuals, character management, and on-screen controls can form a cohesive player experience.
Design focus
Balance the personality of a pixel RPG with readable navigation, character information, and battle controls.
UI/UX Designer — interface layouts, wireframes, visual design, and game UI assets
Personal project · Game UI/UX concept
Completed interface design concept
Figma · AI-assisted visual asset exploration
The challenge

Riftbound brings together several kinds of information: navigation, character details, equipment, rewards, and battle controls. The challenge was to organize these elements clearly while maintaining the personality of a pixel RPG.
The interface needed to feel connected across screens, with enough visual detail to establish the game’s atmosphere while keeping important actions easy to find.
Mapping the experience
The experience centers on three key screens: the lobby, character screen, and battle HUD.
The lobby introduces the game’s main destinations. The character screen focuses on inspecting a hero and their equipment. The battle HUD brings movement controls and abilities into the gameplay view.
Planning these screens helped establish what should receive attention in each context and which visual patterns should remain consistent throughout the interface.
Riftbound lobby screen with the game’s main destinations
Riftbound character screen focused on the selected hero
Riftbound battle HUD with movement controls and abilities
Design decisions
Riftbound lobby interface
Different priorities, one visual language
Each screen serves a different purpose. The lobby emphasizes navigation, the character screen gives more space to the selected hero, and the battle HUD prioritizes controls and visibility.
Shared panel treatments, pixel-style icons, and consistent colors connect these layouts. This allows the composition to change with the player’s task while keeping the interface recognizable.
Riftbound equipment screen with structured item information
Balancing pixel art and readability
Pixel art establishes Riftbound’s identity, but labels, values, and controls still need to be readable at smaller sizes.
The design uses visual hierarchy to separate primary actions from supporting information. Character artwork provides emphasis, while structured panels organize equipment and other details.
The interface
These screens explore the lobby, character management, equipment, and battle HUD as parts of one connected player experience.
Riftbound lobby
Riftbound character screen
Riftbound equipment screen
Riftbound battle HUD
What I learned

This project helped me explore how visual identity and usability influence each other in game interfaces. Small choices in icon detail, typography, and spacing can affect how easily a screen can be understood.
It also highlighted the importance of evaluating controls in context. These screens demonstrate the visual concept, but their usability during actual gameplay still needs validation.
My next step would be to build an interactive prototype and test navigation, icon recognition, and control placement with players.

Project 05 / REAL ESTATE · HOMEPAGE REDESIGN
Marci Metzger Homes
Homepage Redesign

A homepage redesign for Marci Metzger Homes and The Ridge Realty Group, refreshing the existing content with an editorial layout, prominent property photography, and a white-and-earthy palette. The project focuses on a responsive single-page experience—not a full website redesign or live property platform.
Design focus
Refresh the homepage hierarchy while preserving its existing copy and photography across screen sizes.
Homepage Developer
Real Estate Homepage Redesign
Completed
HTML · CSS · JavaScript · Node.js · Vercel
The challenge

Modernize the homepage while preserving the provided copy and existing photography. The challenge was to balance an elevated visual style with clear information hierarchy, helping visitors understand the realtor’s services, explore property imagery, and find contact options across different screen sizes.
Mapping the experience

The homepage supports three visitor needs: getting to know the realtor, exploring what the business offers, and taking the next step. The hero introduces the brand and primary actions, while sales highlights, imagery, and service sections provide more context as visitors scroll. Contact and location options give visitors a clear path to continue their inquiry.

Within this homepage-only scope, listing search remains a labeled preview that directs visitors to the original listings page. The contact form is not connected to a messaging service and offers phone contact instead.
Design decisions
Property photography as the focal point
A large hero image establishes the visual tone, while restrained typography and clear calls to action keep the opening section focused.
An editorial, earthy visual system
White space, olive accents, and rounded imagery give the page a refined but approachable character. Distinct headings and grouped content make longer sections easier to scan.
Responsive layouts with accessible interactions
The layout adapts across mobile, tablet, and desktop. Keyboard focus states, a skip link, and keyboard-accessible gallery controls support navigation beyond mouse interactions.
Subtle motion with practical limits

Scroll reveals and hover effects add movement without dominating the content. Reduced-motion support, lazy-loaded images, and an opt-in map help keep the experience considerate of visitor preferences and loading needs.
The interface
Homepage redesign · View full-size screenshot 1
Homepage redesign · View full-size screenshot 2
What I learned

This project helped me explore how hierarchy, spacing, and typography can refresh a page without replacing its content. It also reinforced that a polished interface depends on more than its desktop appearance—responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and motion preferences deserve attention too.

Working within a homepage-only scope highlighted the importance of communicating limitations clearly. Search previews and disconnected forms should never imply functionality they do not provide. A next step would be usability testing to evaluate how easily visitors understand the page and find their preferred contact option.
